grand_strategy.reading:
Bangladesh is a state between two giants that, for fifteen years, exported its
dependence on one of them and has since 2024 been testing the other. Under
Hasina, security, the border, the water and the grid were handed to India in
exchange for regime protection - 'a blank cheque', as a Dhaka academic put it -
and the cost came due in the uprising of July-August 2024, when the same India
that had underwritten the government became the place where it fled. What
Dhaka has done since is textbook Luttwak at the level of grand strategy: it
converts its single point of leverage, Hasina's person, into a diplomatic
claim, and it widens its menu (Beijing for money and fighters, Islamabad for
a signal, Ankara and Tokyo for industry, Washington for the market) so that
India no longer sets the price. But each widening is paid in the currency India
controls - the Ganges in December, the Teesta, diesel, the 4,096 km border,
the land ports - and India has shown it will use it (April-June 2025). The
BNP government of February 2026 has so far kept both doors ajar: a reset of
tone with Delhi, a four-day state visit to Beijing, and a trade deal with
Washington that the Supreme Court unmade within eleven days. The year-end
tests are concrete and dated: the Ganges Water Treaty lapses in December, LDC
graduation takes effect on 24 November, Rooppur is meant to reach the grid, and
the first Rahman visit to India (set aside around the BRICS summit in New Delhi
in September) has not happened. Two signals that are not rows: Dhaka declined
India's BRICS invitation on the ground of how it was extended (through the
BIMSTEC chair), and India's high commissioner has said he expects the water
and trade questions to move 'once the prime minister visits'. The risk is
that a state which wants to be nobody's client ends up as the disputed ground
between three clients' views of it - India's fear of a China-Pakistan-
Bangladesh convergence at the Siliguri Corridor, China's wish for Mongla and
Teesta, America's wish to see Dhaka not buy arms from Beijing.

stances.note: Why not rival: the BNP government wants the relationship repaired (Rahman's adviser asked for a 'complete reset', the foreign minister went to New Delhi on 7-8 Apr 2026, Dhaka reopened visas for Indians within three days of taking office and asks for more diesel and fertiliser), and Bangladesh cannot do without Indian power (15.6% of supply in 2025), fuel, transit and water. Why not partner: Dhaka resists any alignment ('Bangladesh First', sovereign equality), holds Hasina's extradition (death sentence of 17 Nov 2025; India 'examining' the request in April, July and August 2026) as the price of Rahman's first visit, protests the BSF's border killings (at least 34 in the first 11 months of the interim government) and the pushbacks, and read India's 2025 import restrictions (about USD 770m of trade) as coercion. Cooling since 5 Aug 2026 (Hasina's virtual press conference; the India trip put on hold; BRICS invitation declined 10 Sep). No source uses the exact label; Al Jazeera's reading ('there is no alternative' to dialogue; initial warmth gave way to nationalist rhetoric on both sides) and WPR's ('mild to severe turbulence') are the closest, so the grade is our structural reading (C). Indian-side commentary and ORF are flagged as the Indian view. Bond - grievance: 1971 gratitude has been replaced by a decade of perceived Indian patronage of the Hasina regime, the Ganges and Teesta waters and border deaths.

relations_to.summary: Direct Dhaka-Karachi flights resumed on 29 Jan 2026 after 14 years (Biman Bangladesh Airlines), Islamabad invited Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit after the February 2026 election, and the two prime ministers met in New York in September 2026; JF-17 sale talks held under the interim government have no confirmed contract.

relations_to.summary: Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in Washington on 9 Feb 2026 by the commerce adviser and USTR Greer - 19% tariff, zero duty on garments made with US cotton and man-made fibre, about USD 3.5bn of US farm purchases, USD 15bn of energy over 15 years, 14 Boeing aircraft by Biman, US WTO-reform support, and a clause limiting purchases from countries the US sees as threats. Its tariff base (IEEPA) was struck down by the Supreme Court on 20 Feb 2026.
